# Development

`customer_support.offering.service.development` · offering_type · parent `customer_support.offering.service`

> Custom software built for one client. This is the type where support most closely resembles product support and is most dangerously not it: there is a real artefact, real defects and real reproduction steps, so every product-support instinct feels applicable — but the install base is one, so nothing aggregates and no fix is ever reusable. An organisation that runs this like product support builds an issue tracker, a knowledge base and a deflection programme, and every one of them serves a population of a single customer. The defining dispute is warranty versus enhancement. A client reporting that the software does not do what they need is making a claim that is simultaneously technical and contractual, and the answer turns on the specification rather than on the code. Unlike professional services, where the boundary is about scope of work, here it is about scope of the BUILD, and the evidence is a document written months earlier by people who have moved on. Support is the function that discovers the specification was ambiguous. The second fact is the warranty cliff. Development engagements almost always carry a defined warranty period, after which defect fixes become billable. Nothing about the software or the client's experience changes on that date — only the invoice does — and it is the most contentious moment in the type because the client experiences an identical bug being treated two different ways. A third: the people who can fix anything are the people who built it, and they have been reassigned. Support capacity here is not a queue, it is the availability of a specific small number of engineers whose time is committed elsewhere.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | software written for one client, deployed into their environment or ours, owned by them |
| pricing_shape | fixed fee or time and materials against a specification, with a bounded warranty period and billable support thereafter |
| margin_profile | set at estimation and eroded by warranty work; unbilled defect fixing after handover is the standard way a profitable build becomes a loss |
| post_sale_load | concentrated in the warranty window and dependent entirely on build quality — a well-specified build has almost none and a poorly-specified one never stops |
| support_load | low volume, high specificity, non-delegable. Every ticket needs someone who knows this codebase, and there are few of them |
| resolution_locus | our code, written for exactly one customer. It looks like a product fix and behaves like bespoke labour, because it helps precisely one account |
| notes | The test that resolves most disputes is whether the behaviour contradicts the specification or merely disappoints the client. The first is warranty, the second is an enhancement, and the fact that the specification is usually ambiguous is the real finding.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `expires_at`, `coverage_hours`


> The warranty period is the entitlement, and its expiry is the most contentious date in the engagement: the same defect is free on one side of it and billable on the other, while nothing the client can observe has changed. Modelling the expiry as a first-class fact is what lets the conversation happen before the invoice rather than after it.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.issue`

Requires `product_area_ref`


> Issues here have exactly one affected customer by construction, so the object earns its place for a different reason than in the product tree: it is the record of what the software actually does versus what the specification said, which is the evidence base for every warranty argument.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `resolution_type`, `customer_account_ref`


> resolution_type is where warranty-versus-enhancement is recorded, and it is the number that should feed the next estimate. A development practice that cannot report what fraction of its warranty work was specification ambiguity will keep pricing builds as though it were zero.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> This type is the strongest argument for the offering tree existing at all. It has every surface feature of product support — a codebase, defects, reproductions, releases — and none of the economics, and an organisation that classifies on surface features rather than on resolution_locus will get it wrong in exactly the expensive direction. If the same build is later resold to further clients it stops being this type and becomes a product, and the support model should change with it rather than after it.
